How to Cash a Check Made Out to a Deceased Person in Texas

Short answer

In Texas, a check made out to someone who has died belongs to their estate, so a family member can't simply sign it and deposit it. The usual way is for the court-appointed executor or administrator to deposit it into an estate bank account opened with letters testamentary or letters of administration and an estate EIN. For smaller estates without a will, heirs may be able to collect it with a court-approved small estate affidavit (estate worth $75,000 or less, excluding the homestead and exempt property). A power of attorney ends at death, so the former agent can't cash it. Social Security payments for the month of death or later must be returned.

A refund, a final paycheck, an insurance check: the mail keeps coming after a loved one dies. Banks see these checks every day, and most will refuse them unless the right person brings the right documents. Here's who can cash the check, and how.

Estatethe legal owner of a check payable to the person who died
$75,000Texas small estate affidavit limit, excluding homestead and exempt property
Ends at deatha power of attorney can't be used to cash the check
👉 Don't sign the deceased person's name. Get the authority first, then deposit the check where it belongs.

1Who Can Cash or Deposit the Check

Executor or administratorAppointed by the probate court and given letters testamentary or letters of administration. Deposits the check into an estate account.
Heirs with a small estate affidavitFor estates without a will worth $75,000 or less, excluding the homestead and exempt property, once a judge approves the affidavit.
A co-payeeIf the check is payable to two people, the bank's rules decide whether the survivor can deposit it, often with a death certificate.
Not the power of attorneyUnder Texas law a durable power of attorney ends when the principal dies. See power of attorney after death.

If a will exists, it may be probated as a muniment of title without an executor; some banks accept the court order to release funds. When there's no will, an affidavit of heirship may help identify the heirs.

2Common Checks After a Death, and What to Do

  • Social Security: benefits aren't payable for the month of death. A check for that month or later must be returned, and direct deposits should be sent back through the bank.
  • Federal tax refund: a surviving spouse filing jointly or the estate's representative can claim it; others generally file IRS Form 1310.
  • Final paycheck, refunds and insurance checks: usually estate assets, deposited into the estate account or collected through a small estate affidavit.
  • Life insurance or retirement accounts with a named beneficiary: paid directly to the beneficiary, outside probate.

3Opening an Estate Account

  1. Get appointed by the probate court and obtain certified letters testamentary or administration.
  2. Get an EIN for the estate from the IRS. See EIN for an estate in Texas.
  3. Bring a death certificate, the letters and your ID to the bank.
  4. Deposit the check into the estate account and keep records for the accounting.

Executors can't put estate checks into their own accounts. Read can you deposit an estate check into a personal account.

4Mistakes That Cause Problems

  • Signing the deceased person's name on the check, which can be treated as forgery
  • Using the old power of attorney after the death
  • Cashing a Social Security check for the month of death
  • Depositing into a personal or joint account without authority, which can create disputes with other heirs
  • Waiting too long: banks may refuse checks older than six months

?Frequently Asked Questions

Can I cash a check made out to a deceased person in Texas?

Only with legal authority. The executor or administrator can deposit it into an estate account, or heirs can collect it with a court-approved small estate affidavit if the estate qualifies.

Can a power of attorney cash a check after death?

No. Under Texas Estates Code Section 751.131, a durable power of attorney terminates when the principal dies, so the agent loses authority to handle the person's money.

What do I do with a Social Security check after someone dies?

Return it. Social Security is not payable for the month of death, so any check for that month or later must be sent back, and direct deposits should be returned through the bank.

Can I deposit a deceased person's check into their own bank account?

Usually not. Once the bank learns of the death, the account is typically restricted until someone shows legal authority, and joint or payable-on-death accounts pass to the surviving owner or beneficiary. Checks payable to the deceased should go into an estate account opened by the executor or administrator.

What if the estate is small?

If there is no will and the estate is worth $75,000 or less, excluding the homestead and exempt property, heirs may use a small estate affidavit after 30 days, once a judge approves it.

The right paperwork gets it where it belongs.

Sources: Texas Estates Code § 751.131 · TexasLawHelp – Small Estate Affidavits · Social Security Administration – Survivors Benefits · IRS – About Form 1310 · TexasLawHelp – Handling an Estate. This article is general information, not legal advice.

Before proceeding, please review the\u00a0 legal disclaimer.

Can You Cash or Deposit a Deceased Person\u2019s Check in Texas? (2025 Guide)

Finding a check made out to someone who has passed away can create immediate confusion.

A lot of people assume:

\ud83d\udc49 \u201cI\u2019m the spouse/child/executor, so I should be able to deposit it.\u201d

Unfortunately, it usually isn\u2019t that simple.

Banks are extremely cautious when it comes to checks issued to deceased individuals\u2014and handling them incorrectly can create legal and financial problems.

Let\u2019s walk through what happens to a deceased person\u2019s check in Texas, who can handle it, and what steps should be taken next.

What Happens to a Check After Someone Dies?

When a person passes away, checks made payable to them generally become part of their estate.

That means:

  • The funds do not automatically belong to family members

  • The check usually cannot simply be deposited into someone else\u2019s account

  • The estate may need to process the funds properly through probate or estate administration

Can You Deposit a Deceased Person\u2019s Check?

In many cases:

\ud83d\udc49 Not directly.

Whether a check can be deposited depends on:

  • The type of check

  • The size of the estate

  • Whether probate has been opened

  • Who has legal authority to act for the estate

Banks often freeze or closely review accounts once they learn of a death.

Who Has Authority to Handle the Check?

Typically, the person with legal authority over the estate can handle the funds.

This may include:

  • The executor named in a will

  • A court-appointed administrator

  • In some cases, a surviving joint account holder

Without proper authority, cashing or depositing the check may create legal issues.

Common Types of Checks Received After Death

Several kinds of checks commonly arrive after someone passes away.

1. Refund Checks

Examples:

  • Utility refunds

  • Insurance reimbursements

  • Tax refunds

2. Final Paychecks

Employers may issue:

  • Remaining wages

  • Vacation payouts

  • Bonuses

Texas employers often require additional documentation before reissuing or releasing funds.

3. Social Security Checks

This is important:

\ud83d\udc49 Social Security payments issued after death may need to be returned.

Improperly cashing these checks can create serious problems.

4. Insurance or Benefit Checks

Some checks may already have designated beneficiaries and avoid probate entirely.

Others may belong to the estate.

What If the Check Was Issued Before Death?

This is where people get confused.

Even if:

  • The check was written before death

  • The person simply didn\u2019t cash it yet

\ud83d\udc49 The check may still need to be handled through the estate after death occurs.

Banks often will not process it normally once notified of the death.

Can You Deposit the Check Into the Deceased Person\u2019s Account?

Usually, no\u2014or at least not without complications.

Many banks:

  • Freeze individual accounts upon notice of death

  • Restrict access until estate authority is verified

If probate is opened, the executor may instead:

  • Open an estate account

  • Deposit the funds there

What Is an Estate Account?

An estate account is a bank account opened by the executor or administrator to manage estate funds.

This account is often used for:

  • Depositing checks payable to the deceased

  • Paying debts and expenses

  • Distributing funds to beneficiaries

What Documents May Be Required?

Banks commonly ask for:

  • Death certificate

  • Letters Testamentary or Letters of Administration

  • Identification

  • Possibly a copy of the will

Requirements vary depending on:

  • The bank

  • The size of the check

  • The type of estate administration involved

What Happens If Someone Cashes the Check Improperly?

This can create major issues.

Potential problems include:

  • Claims from other heirs or beneficiaries

  • Banking fraud concerns

  • Demands to repay funds

  • Delays in probate administration

Even innocent mistakes can create complications later.

Are Small Estates Treated Differently?

Sometimes.

Texas offers certain simplified procedures for smaller estates, depending on:

  • The total estate value

  • The type of assets involved

But even in small estates, checks payable to the deceased should be handled carefully.

How The Lange Firm Helps With Estate Administration

At The Lange Firm, we help Texas families navigate the practical and legal issues that arise after a loved one passes away.

That includes:

  • Probate and estate administration

  • Determining who has authority to handle assets

  • Addressing banking and financial issues

  • Helping avoid costly mistakes during the process

Because even something as simple as a check can become complicated after death.

Final Takeaway

If you receive a check payable to someone who has passed away:

\ud83d\udc49 Don\u2019t rush to cash or deposit it.

The correct process depends on:

  • The type of check

  • Whether probate is required

  • Who has legal authority over the estate

Handled properly, these issues can usually be resolved smoothly.

Handled incorrectly, they can create unnecessary legal and financial complications for the family.
